entries.question: Did God commend or condemn Jehu for the killings at Jezreel?
entries.summary: 2 Kings 9:6-8 has God commission Jehu to wipe out the house of Ahab, an instruction Jehu carries out with extreme violence at Jezreel. Hosea 1:4 has the same God announce he will avenge "the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu" — meaning he will punish Jehu's dynasty for the very killings he ordered.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the sharpest moral-theological contradictions in the Hebrew Bible. The Deuteronomistic narrator in 2 Kings 9 has Yahweh anoint Jehu through a prophet of Elisha and explicitly command him to slaughter Ahab's house. Jehu obeys: he kills Joram of Israel, Ahaziah of Judah, Jezebel, the seventy sons of Ahab, Ahaziah's relatives, and the prophets of Baal. The narrator endorses this in 2 Kings 10:30 — "because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes."

Then Hosea 1:4 happens. The prophet Hosea — writing roughly a century later — names his son Jezreel and declares that Yahweh will "avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel." The same God who ordered the killings now treats them as bloodguilt requiring vengeance.

The apologist harmonization, defended by Hans Walter Wolff cautiously and by Duane Garrett more forcefully in the NAC Hosea volume, draws a distinction between the act commanded and the manner executed. Jehu was commissioned to remove Ahab's house. He was not commissioned to massacre with the brutality and overreach he displayed — killing Ahaziah, all the prophets, and beyond what divine sanction covered. Hosea condemns the excess, not the obedience.

That reading has some weight. Jehu did exceed his mandate. But it leaves a problem: 2 Kings 10:30 explicitly says Yahweh approved Jehu's conduct as "right." If the manner was wrong, the Deuteronomist didn't get the memo. Critical scholars from Wolff to Marvin Sweeney to Francis Andersen and David Noel Freedman in the AB Hosea read this as competing theological evaluations from different periods. The Deuteronomist celebrated Jehu's purge as covenant fidelity; Hosea, a century into the consequences, read the same purge as bloody dynastic crime requiring divine reckoning. Same act, contradictory canonical verdicts.

Verdict: the surface contradiction is real and the manner-vs-mandate harmonization works only by ignoring 2 Kings 10:30. Critical scholarship treats this as evidence of competing theological perspectives within the canon — not a logical error so much as a moral evolution.

answers.answer_explanation: Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, I have anointed thee king over the people of the Lord, even over Israel. And thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the Lord, at the hand of Jezebel. For the whole house of Ahab shall perish: and I will cut off from Ahab him that pisseth against the wall. 2 Kings 9:6-8

And the LORD said unto him, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel. Hosea 1:4

commentary_out.commentary:
This is among the sharpest moral-theological contradictions in the Hebrew Bible because the two verdicts concern the same act and are both attributed to Yahweh. In 2 Kings 9:6-8 a member of Elisha's prophetic guild anoints Jehu and delivers an explicit divine commission to annihilate the house of Ahab "that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets" shed by Jezebel. Jehu executes the coup with thoroughness: he kills Joram of Israel, Ahaziah of Judah, Jezebel, the seventy sons of Ahab in Samaria, forty-two kinsmen of Ahaziah, the surviving adherents of the Omride court, and the assembled worshippers of Baal whom he lures into a temple and slaughters. Crucially, the Deuteronomistic narrator does not merely report this; in 2 Kings 10:30 Yahweh commends it: "Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes, and hast done unto the house of Ahab according to all that was in mine heart, thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel." The dynastic reward is the Historian's own theological endorsement, and it explains why the Jehu dynasty in fact lasted four generations (Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II, Zechariah).

Roughly a century later, Hosea 1:4 reverses the verdict. Hosea names his firstborn Jezreel and announces that Yahweh will "avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel." "The blood of Jezreel" points directly at the bloodbath of the coup — Jezreel was where Joram and Jezebel died — and the announced punishment fell on Zechariah, the fourth-generation heir whose murder ended the dynasty (2 Kings 15:10-12). The God who promised the dynasty as a reward for the killings now treats the killings as bloodguilt demanding the dynasty's extinction.

The strongest harmonization, articulated cautiously by Hans Walter Wolff and more confidently by Duane Garrett in the New American Commentary, distinguishes the mandate from the manner. Jehu was authorized to remove Ahab's house but exceeded the commission in scope and motive — slaughtering Ahaziah and his kin (a Judahite, outside the Israelite mandate), the Baal worshippers en masse, and acting from political ambition rather than covenant zeal. Hosea, on this reading, condemns the excess and the self-serving bloodlust, not the obedience. The argument has real textual purchase: Jehu plainly overreached, and 2 Kings 10:31 immediately notes that he himself did not keep the law or abandon the calf-cult, undercutting any portrait of him as a righteous agent.

What the harmonization cannot absorb is 2 Kings 10:30. The Deuteronomist does not say Jehu did the right thing badly; he says Jehu did "that which is right in mine eyes" and "according to all that was in mine heart," and rewards him for it. If the manner was the offense, the Historian betrays no awareness of it. The cleaner explanation, advanced by Wolff, Andersen and Freedman in the Anchor Bible Hosea, and Marvin Sweeney, is diachronic: two theological traditions evaluate one purge from opposite ends of its consequences. The Deuteronomistic source celebrated Jehu's coup as covenant fidelity and Yahwistic house-cleaning; Hosea, witnessing the violence, instability, and Assyrian pressure that the dynasty's century ultimately produced, read the founding massacre as a crime that Yahweh would requite. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, which depicts "Jehu son of Omri" (Iaua mar Humri) prostrate and paying tribute, situates the dynasty in its real geopolitical squeeze — and it is the secure epigraphic attestation here. The Tel Dan Stele, sometimes dragged into this discussion, does not name Jehu at all and its bearing on the coup is debated (it most plausibly has an Aramean king claiming the deaths of Joram and Ahaziah), so the Black Obelisk, not Tel Dan, is the load-bearing extra-biblical evidence.

Verdict: a genuine contradiction in canonical evaluation. The manner-versus-mandate harmonization founders on 2 Kings 10:30's unqualified divine approval; the data are best explained as competing theological judgments from different periods preserved side by side in the canon.

entries.question: Who succeeded Jehoiakim as king?
entries.summary: 2 Kings 24:6 records that Jehoiakim slept with his fathers and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his stead. Jeremiah 36:30 declares that Jehoiakim "shall have none to sit upon the throne of David" — meaning no son should succeed him.
entries.commentary:
2 Kings 24:6 gives the standard succession formula: Jehoiakim died, his son Jehoiachin took the throne. Jeremiah 36:30, in an earlier oracle pronounced against Jehoiakim for burning Jeremiah's scroll, says Yahweh has decreed Jehoiakim will have "none to sit upon the throne of David" — meaning no descendant will hold the Davidic monarchy.

The standard apologetic harmonization — Jack Lundbom in the AB volumes on Jeremiah, F.B. Huey in the NAC — argues Jehoiachin's three-month reign doesn't really count as "sitting upon the throne of David." Three months and ten days before exile to Babylon is a technicality, not a real reign. Walter Brueggemann in his Jeremiah commentary takes a similar line: the prophetic oracle envisages a substantive enthronement, which Jehoiachin never achieved before deportation.

There's something to this. Jehoiachin's reign was nominal. He was a teenager (per 2 Kings 24:8 — see id 299 for the age problem) who reigned for three months before Nebuchadnezzar carted him to Babylon. He never exercised meaningful royal authority. So Jeremiah's oracle might be loosely true if you read "throne" as substantive enthronement rather than formal succession.

But the harmonization runs into trouble. The text of 2 Kings 24:6 uses the exact formula it uses for every other Davidic succession — "reigned in his stead" (malak takhtaiw). Jehoiachin is enumerated in subsequent royal genealogies and the Chronicler counts him as a king. He sits on the throne of David in the technical, formal, narrative sense. Jack Lundbom and William Holladay both concede the Jeremiah oracle was either falsified by Jehoiachin's brief succession or required radical reinterpretation. Holladay in the Hermeneia Jeremiah volume reads it as a prophetic oracle that didn't quite come true and had to be theologically rescued by redefining "throne."

The deeper issue: 1 Chronicles 3:17-18 lists Jehoiachin's seven sons born in exile, and Matthew 1:11-12 puts Jehoiachin's son Shealtiel in Jesus' Davidic genealogy. The Davidic line ran through Jehoiakim's son, even into exile. Jeremiah's curse was either prematurely lifted or never literally fulfilled.

Verdict: the harmonization works by redefining "throne" as substantive rule, which the text doesn't stipulate. On the plain succession-language of 2 Kings 24:6, Jehoiakim was succeeded by his son — exactly what Jeremiah said wouldn't happen.

answers.answer: He was succeeded as king by his son.
answers.answer_explanation:
So Jehoiachim slept with his fathers; and Jehoiachin his son
				          reigned in his stead. 2 Kings 24:6

answers.answer: He had no one to succeed him.
answers.answer_explanation:
Therefore thus saith the Lord of Jehoiakim king of Judah; He
				          shall have none to sit upon the throne of David. Jeremiah 36:30

commentary_out.commentary:
Second Kings 24:6 records the conventional succession: Jehoiakim 'slept with his fathers,' and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his stead (the verb is malak takhtaiv, the formulaic notice used throughout the regnal framework). Jeremiah 36:30, by contrast, pronounces a curse on Jehoiakim for burning the prophet's scroll — an episode datable to the fourth or fifth year of Jehoiakim, around 604 BCE, well before his death — declaring that he 'shall have none to sit upon the throne of David,' and that his corpse will be cast out unburied. On the surface the prediction that no descendant would occupy the Davidic throne collides with the report that his son immediately succeeded him.

The strongest harmonization, advanced by Jack Lundbom in the Anchor Bible, F.B. Huey in the New American Commentary, and Walter Brueggemann, reads the oracle as targeting substantive, enduring Davidic rule rather than the bare formality of accession. Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah and Coniah) reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar deported him to Babylon in 597 BCE; he was a youth (2 Kings 24:8) who exercised no meaningful royal authority and presided over no policy. On this view the oracle envisages real enthronement and dynastic continuity, neither of which Jehoiachin achieved, so the prophecy holds in the sense its defenders intend. This is a genuine reading, not a dodge — Hebrew prophetic curses of this kind regularly concern the durability of a house rather than the technicalities of succession, and Jeremiah 22:30 makes the point explicit about Coniah: 'no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah,' which clearly contemplates effective rule, not mere coronation.

The difficulty is that 2 Kings 24:6 does not stipulate any distinction between formal and substantive rule. It applies to Jehoiachin the same succession formula it applies to every Davidic king, the regnal framework in 24:8 supplies his accession age and reign length as it does for any monarch, and both the Chronicler and the canon enumerate him among the kings of Judah. To the narrator he sat on the throne of David in precisely the formal sense the language conveys. Lundbom and William Holladay both acknowledge that the oracle was either rendered inexact by Jehoiachin's brief accession or required reinterpretation to survive; Holladay treats it as a prophetic word that history did not straightforwardly confirm and that later tradition theologically rescued by narrowing 'throne' to mean lasting dominion.

The genealogical afterlife of the line sharpens the problem. First Chronicles 3:17-18 lists Jehoiachin's seven sons born in Babylon, the Babylonian administrative ration tablets (the Weidner texts) name Yaukin/Jehoiachin of Judah among recipients of royal provisions in Babylon, confirming his survival in exile, and 2 Kings 25:27-30 reports his release and elevation above other captive kings under Evil-Merodach. Matthew 1:11-12 then routes the Davidic-messianic line through Jehoiachin to Shealtiel and Zerubbabel — and the post-exilic governor Zerubbabel becomes a focus of restoration hope (Haggai 2:23, where he is Yahweh's 'signet,' pointedly reversing the signet-imagery of the curse in Jeremiah 22:24). The Davidic line not only continued through Jehoiakim's son but was theologically central to later expectation, which means the curse of Jeremiah 36:30, taken at full strength, was either never literally realized or was understood to have been mitigated.

Verdict: partially harmonizable — 'throne of David' can be read as substantive, durable rule that Jehoiachin's three-month puppet reign never constituted — but the resolution requires narrowing the term in a way 2 Kings 24:6 does not authorize, and on the plain succession-language Jehoiakim was succeeded by his son, exactly what the oracle denied.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The oracle in Jeremiah 36:30 plausibly targets enduring, substantive Davidic rule, and Jehoiachin's three-month puppet reign before deportation arguably did not constitute 'sitting on the throne of David' in that sense; but 2 Kings 24:6 uses the standard succession formula and the canon counts Jehoiachin among the kings, so the resolution depends on a non-stipulated narrowing of 'throne.'

entries.question: Who was Zechariah's father?
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles 24:20-21 narrates the stoning of Zechariah son of Jehoiada "in the court of the house of the Lord" — exactly the death scenario Jesus references in Matthew 23:35. But Matthew calls the victim "Zacharias son of Barachias." So either Jesus (or Matthew) has the wrong father's name for the high-profile temple-court murder, or the Gospel is referring to a different Zechariah entirely.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction has bothered Christian commentators since antiquity. Jerome already noted the problem in the fourth century. The scenario Jesus describes — a Zechariah murdered between the temple and the altar — fits 2 Chronicles 24 exactly. That is the only canonical Hebrew Bible account of a priest-prophet being killed in the temple courtyard. The problem is that the 2 Chronicles Zechariah is the son of Jehoiada, while Matthew's Zechariah is the son of Barachias.

The apologist harmonization branches into several attempts. Archer's main move is to argue that Jehoiada had two names — Jehoiada and Barachias — or that Barachias was Jehoiada's father, making Jehoiada the grandfather rather than the father of this Zechariah, and Matthew is using "son of" in the looser ancestral sense. There is zero textual evidence for any of this. The 2 Chronicles narrative names only Jehoiada as Zechariah's father, and the Hebrew Bible elsewhere never refers to Jehoiada as Barachias or vice versa. A second harmonization, advanced by some traditional commentators, is that Jesus is referring to Zechariah the prophet (the post-exilic prophet of the book of Zechariah), whose father was Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). That is a closer name match, but Zechariah the prophet was not murdered in the temple — there is no biblical or extra-biblical record of his death by stoning. So this harmonization rescues the name at the cost of breaking the death scenario.

The critical reading, developed in detail by Davies and Allison in their ICC Matthew and by Raymond Brown in The Death of the Messiah, is that Matthew has confused or conflated two Zechariahs. The author of Matthew was working with the figure from 2 Chronicles (whose death scenario Jesus references) but supplied the wrong patronymic — possibly cross-pollinating from Zechariah the prophet, or from Zechariah son of Baris, an eminent citizen murdered by Zealots in the temple courts during the Jewish War (Josephus, War 4.335-344, c. 67-68 CE). Several critical scholars including Dale Allison have noted that the Josephus parallel is striking enough that Matthew may even be reading Christian persecution backwards into Jesus' speech. Whatever the source of the confusion, the simplest explanation is that the author of Matthew got the patronymic wrong.

The verdict is that the contradiction is real and the harmonizations are post-hoc patches. Either Matthew has erred on the patronymic, or Jesus is referring to a temple-courtyard murder we have no other record of involving a Barachias-fathered Zechariah, which is a counsel of desperation. The cleanest reading is that the Gospel writer confused two figures named Zechariah — a perfectly normal mistake for any human author working without access to a unified database of biblical priests.

answers.answer_explanation:
And the spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada
				          .... And they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the
				          commandment of the king in the court of the house of the lord. 2 Chronicles 24:20-21

Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the
				          temple and the altar. Matthew 23:35

commentary_out.commentary:
This contradiction has troubled Christian commentators since antiquity; Jerome already flagged it in the fourth century, noting that the Gospel of the Nazarenes read "son of Jehoiada." The death scenario Jesus describes in Matthew 23:35 — a Zechariah murdered "between the sanctuary and the altar" — matches 2 Chronicles 24:20-21 precisely, the only canonical Hebrew Bible account of a priest-prophet stoned in the temple court, and a resonant one on the prevailing scholarly reading because Chronicles stood last in the Jewish canonical order, making Abel-to-Zechariah a sweep from Genesis to the final book ("from A to Z"). That ordering is the explanation Luz and most commentators favor, though it should be flagged as a widely-held hypothesis rather than a certainty, since the canonical sequence in the first century is not firmly fixed and the Chronicles-stood-last arrangement is securely attested only in later tradition (b. Bava Batra 14b). The dying Zechariah of 2 Chronicles even cries, "May the LORD see and avenge!" (24:22), which Jesus's blood-guilt saying echoes. The difficulty is the patronymic: 2 Chronicles names him son of Jehoiada the priest, while Matthew calls him "son of Barachiah." Tellingly, the Lukan parallel (Luke 11:51) names the same Zechariah and the same death but supplies no father's name at all, which many scholars take as evidence that the patronymic in Matthew is a secondary, and erroneous, expansion.

The apologetic harmonizations branch. Archer proposes that Jehoiada bore two names, or that Barachiah was Jehoiada's father, so "son of" means grandson or descendant. There is no textual support: the Hebrew Bible never links Jehoiada with the name Barachiah. A second route identifies the victim as Zechariah the post-exilic prophet, "son of Berechiah" (Zech 1:1) — a near-exact name match. But there is no record, biblical or otherwise, of that prophet being martyred in the temple; this rescues the patronymic only by abandoning the death scenario that anchors the saying. A third route appeals to Jewish tradition: the Targum to Lamentations 2:20 and several rabbinic texts (e.g. the traditions surveyed by Sheldon Blank) recount the murder of "Zechariah son of Iddo, the priest and prophet" in the temple, and rabbinic memory itself conflated the Chronicles priest with the prophet, since the prophet Zechariah is called "son of Berechiah son of Iddo" (Zech 1:1) while Ezra 5:1 calls him "son of Iddo." That conflation in Jewish tradition is real — but it is evidence that the two Zechariahs were already being merged, not that they were one person.

The critical reading, developed by Davies and Allison in their ICC Matthew and Raymond Brown in The Death of the Messiah, is that Matthew (or his tradition) conflated two figures: he intends the Chronicles martyr, whose death scenario he reproduces, but attaches the prophet's patronymic, "son of Berechiah/Barachiah." A further candidate, raised by Dale Allison and others, is the Zechariah whose patronymic in Josephus is textually uncertain — commonly printed "son of Baris," though the manuscripts are corrupt at this point and the name should not be presented as fixed — a prominent Jerusalemite murdered by Zealots in the temple court during the Jewish War, recorded by Josephus (War 4.334-344, c. 67-68 CE), close enough in name, place, and manner that some suspect Matthew, writing after 70 CE, read a recent atrocity back into Jesus's words, though the chronology makes direct dependence debated.

Verdict: a genuine error of identification, almost certainly a conflation of two (possibly three) men named Zechariah. The harmonizations either invent an undocumented double name, or save the name at the cost of the temple-court death, or rest on a Jewish tradition that itself reflects the same conflation. The absence of any patronymic in the Lukan parallel makes the simplest explanation — that Matthew's "son of Barachiah" is a mistaken expansion — the most probable.

entries.question: Did Jehoiakim die in Babylon or near Jerusalem?
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles 36:5-6 says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim in fetters "to carry him to Babylon." Jeremiah 22:18-19 prophesies that Jehoiakim will receive the burial of an ass and be "cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem." The implication of Chronicles is that he was carried off to Babylon; Jeremiah specifies an ignominious burial just outside Jerusalem. Both passages cannot be plainly accurate without rewriting one of them.
entries.commentary:
What makes this contradiction particularly thorny is that even the historical record outside the Bible is unclear about how Jehoiakim died. 2 Kings 24:6 says only that "Jehoiakim slept with his fathers" — the standard biblical euphemism for peaceful death and burial — and gives no location. The Babylonian Chronicle for Nebuchadnezzar's reign confirms an attack on Judah around 598 BCE but does not specify Jehoiakim's fate. So we are working with three biblical traditions and external silence, and the three biblical traditions don't agree.

The apologist harmonization, advanced by Archer and Kaiser, is to argue that 2 Chronicles only describes Nebuchadnezzar's intent to take Jehoiakim to Babylon, not that the trip was completed. The Hebrew laholikho babelah ("to bring him to Babylon") is an infinitive expressing purpose — Nebuchadnezzar bound him intending to deport him but Jehoiakim died en route or in Jerusalem before deportation occurred. That is actually a defensible reading of the syntax. The infinitive construct can express purpose. But the Chronicler's narrative goes on to describe other temple vessels being carried off to Babylon in the next breath, framing Jehoiakim as part of the same general deportation event. The reader is left with the impression that he ended up in Babylon, even if the grammar formally leaves it open.

The critical reading, found in Cogan and Tadmor's Anchor Bible II Kings (working from the Kings parallel), and developed for Chronicles by Sara Japhet and Ralph Klein, treats the three accounts as preserving divergent traditions about how a Judahite king who resisted Babylonian power died. Lundbom in his Anchor Bible Jeremiah notes that the Jeremiah 22:18-19 prophecy is harsh and probably reflects either an actual ignominious death or a piece of prophetic invective that did not literally come to pass (the Hebrew Bible is full of unfulfilled prophecies, despite traditional claims otherwise). The Chronicler, writing centuries later, smoothed over the harsh Jeremiah tradition by replacing the disgraceful burial with a vaguer fetters-and-deportation scenario. 2 Kings split the difference with the formulaic "slept with his fathers," which usually implies peaceful succession.

The verdict is that we have three different biblical pictures and no way to reconcile them without straining one or another. The harmonization that Chronicles only describes Nebuchadnezzar's intent is grammatically possible but contextually weak. The simplest reading is that different biblical writers preserved different traditions about a king whose death was, evidently, not well-remembered. That is a perfectly human explanation for the kind of textual divergence we actually see.

				          his God. Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and bound
				          him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon. 2 Chronicles 36:5-6

commentary_out.commentary:
The difficulty here is compounded by the fact that the external and internal record of how Jehoiakim died is genuinely murky, and three biblical traditions diverge. 2 Kings 24:6 reports only that "Jehoiakim slept with his fathers" (wayishkav... im-avotaw) — the conventional formula for ordinary death and dynastic burial — and gives no location and no notice of deportation. The Babylonian Chronicle (BM 21946) documents Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against "the city of Judah" and the capture of its king in his seventh year (March 597 BCE), but that captured king is Jehoiachin, Jehoiakim's son and successor, not Jehoiakim himself, who appears to have died shortly before the city fell. So the cuneiform evidence does not directly settle Jehoiakim's fate, and the three biblical sources fill the gap differently.

2 Chronicles 36:5-6 states that Nebuchadnezzar "bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon" (le-holikho babelah), juxtaposed immediately with the removal of temple vessels to Babylon. Jeremiah 22:18-19, by contrast, delivers a savage oracle: Jehoiakim will receive "the burial of a donkey" — dragged off and flung beyond the gates of Jerusalem, unmourned. The two pictures are difficult to reconcile: a deportee to Babylon versus a corpse dumped outside the capital.

The apologetic harmonization, defended by Archer and Kaiser, fastens on the grammar of Chronicles. The phrase le-holikho is an infinitive construct expressing purpose: Nebuchadnezzar bound him intending to deport him, without the text asserting the deportation was completed. On this reading Jehoiakim could have died in or near Jerusalem before being carried off, leaving room for the Jeremiah oracle to stand. This is grammatically legitimate — the purpose-infinitive does not entail fulfillment. The contextual weakness is that the Chronicler immediately narrates the temple vessels going to Babylon in the same sentence, building a cumulative impression of a deportation event in which the bound king is naturally included; the casual reader is left believing Jehoiakim went to Babylon, even if the syntax stops short of saying so.

The critical reading, found in Cogan and Tadmor's Anchor Bible II Kings (on the parallel) and developed for Chronicles by Sara Japhet and Ralph Klein, treats the three accounts as competing traditions about an awkward death. Jack Lundbom, in his Anchor Bible Jeremiah, observes that the donkey-burial oracle in Jeremiah 22 is invective whose literal fulfillment is unverified — and the Hebrew Bible preserves prophetic threats that did not come to pass as stated. The Chronicler, writing in the Persian period, likely smoothed the embarrassing Jeremianic tradition by substituting a vaguer fetters-and-deportation notice, while Kings used the neutral death-formula. William Holladay's Hermeneia Jeremiah similarly reads 22:18-19 as a rhetorically charged threat rather than a chronicle of fact.

It is worth noting that 2 Chronicles 36:6 does not actually say Jehoiakim died in Babylon; the question's framing infers it. But even granting the cautious infinitive reading, the texts do not cohere into a single account: Jeremiah's contemptuous unburied-corpse-outside-Jerusalem and Chronicles' fettered-king-bound-for-Babylon pull in incompatible directions, and Kings' peaceful "slept with his fathers" agrees with neither. The harmonization can defuse the narrow claim that Chronicles asserts death in Babylon, but it cannot reconcile the substance of the Jeremiah oracle with the Chronicles narrative or with Kings. Verdict: partially harmonizable on the grammar of Chronicles, but the three traditions remain in genuine, unresolved tension over Jehoiakim's actual fate.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The Chronicles phrase le-holikho babelah is a purpose infinitive ('to carry him') that does not assert the deportation was completed, so Chronicles need not claim Jehoiakim died in Babylon; this defuses the narrow 'died in Babylon vs. near Jerusalem' framing, but the substantive clash between Jeremiah's unburied-corpse oracle, the Chronicler's fetters narrative, and the neutral 'slept with his fathers' of 2 Kings 24:6 remains unresolved.
